exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule

question.explanation:
Note that plugging in $x = 0$ gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

\begin{align*} \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\ln\!\left(1+\sin(4x)\right)}{\tan(2x)} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left[\ln\!\left(1+\sin(4x)\right)\right]'}{[\tan(2x)]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac {\left(\dfrac{4\cos(4x)}{1+\sin(4x)}\right)}{2\sec^2(2x)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\left(\dfrac{4\cos(4(0))}{1+\sin(4(0))}\right)}{2\sec^2(2(0))}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\left(\dfrac{4(1)}{1+0}\right)}{2(1)}\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule

question.explanation:
Note that plugging in $x = 16$ gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

\begin{align*} \lim_{x \to 16} \dfrac{x^2 - 20x + 64}{\sqrt{x} - 4} & = \lim_{x \to 16} \dfrac{[x^2 - 20x + 64]'}{[\sqrt{x} - 4]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x\to 16} \dfrac {2x-20}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {2(16)-20}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{16}}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {32-20}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2(4)}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {12}{\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right)}\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{96} \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

question.explanation:
If we plug in $x = 0$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit: \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1+5x)-5x}{x^2} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\left[\ln(1+5x)-5x\right]'}{[x^2]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{5}{1+5x}-5\right)}{2x}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{5}{2}\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{1+5x}-1\right)}{x} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\ln(1+5x)-5x}{x^2} & = \dfrac{5}{2}\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{1}{1+5x}-1\right)}{x}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{5}{2}\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left[(1+5x)^{-1}-1 \right]'}{[x]'}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{5}{2}\lim_{x \to 0} \left(-5(1+5x)^{-2}\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(-5\right)\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{25}{2}}. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

question.explanation:
If we plug in $x = 0$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit: \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{e^{8x} - e^{5x} - 3x}{x^2} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left[e^{8x} - e^{5x} - 3x\right]'}{[x^2]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{8e^{8x} - 5e^{5x} - 3}{2x} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{e^{8x} - e^{5x} - 3x}{x^2} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{8e^{8x} - 5e^{5x} - 3}{2x}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\left[8e^{8x} - 5e^{5x} - 3\right]'}{[2x]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{64e^{8x} - 25e^{5x}}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{64(1) - 25(1)}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{39}{2}. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

question.explanation:
If we plug in $x = 2$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

\begin{align} \lim_{x\to2} \dfrac{(x^2-3)^2-8x+15}{x^2-4x+4} & = \lim_{x\to2} \dfrac{\left[ (x^2-3)^2-8x+15 \right]'}{\left[ x^2-4x+4 \right]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x\to2} \dfrac{4x(x^2 - 3) - 8}{2x - 4} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get \begin{align} \lim_{x\to2} \dfrac{(x^2-3)^2-8x+15}{x^2-4x+4} & = \lim_{x\to2} \dfrac{4x(x^2 - 3) - 8}{2x - 4}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x\to2} \dfrac{\left[4x(x^2 - 3) - 8\right]'}{\left[2x - 4\right]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x\to2} \dfrac{4(x^2 - 3) + 8x^2}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4(2^2 - 3) + 8(2)^2}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4 + 32}{2}\\[5pt] & = 18. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

question.explanation:
If we plug in $x = 0$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit: \begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^2}{e^{x}-x-1} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{[x^2]'}{[e^{x}-x-1]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2x}{e^x-1} \end{align}

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

\begin{align} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^2}{x-1+e^{x}} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2x}{e^x - 1}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{[2x]'}{[e^x-1]'}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2}{e^x}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{e^{0}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{1}\\[5pt] & = 2. \end{align}
